extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying patent scope and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when a discovered principle, law of nature, or new application of a known principle is patentable, and on the proper scope and limits of claims (including examples and case-law).

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for an abstract principle; patentable when coupled with a mode
rubrics_metrics.description: "You cannot take out a patent for a principle; you may take out a patent for a principle coupled with the mode of carrying the principle into effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor must have invented some mode of carrying the principle into effect; where a principle is merely stated apart from a special purpose or practical operation it is an abstract principle and not patentable. (Quoted in Jupe's patent discussion; see also Neilson and the analysis of Morse.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protection for principle plus a disclosed practical mode may extend to other modes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where a person discovers a principle or property of nature, or ... a new application ... and also of some mode of carrying it out into practice, so as to produce or attain a new and useful effect or result, he is entitled to protection against all other modes of carrying the same principle or property into practice for obtaining the same effect or result."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means and machinery are material only so far as they effect the identity of the application; if the patentee has pointed out a mode and not tied himself to the particular mode, courts have treated piracy of other modes as infringement (cases cited: Jupe, Neilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of claim is not necessarily fatal if it is within the stated object and benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: "This generality of claim, that is, for all modes of applying the principle to the purpose specified, according to or within a general statement of the object to be attained...is no objection to the patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent fairly states the object and the use to be made of the agent, and the application or use can be carried out in a variety of ways, the broad wording may reflect the comprehensiveness and be upheld (Lord Justice in Neilson's case).

rubrics_metrics.name: A new application of a well-known law of nature producing a practical result is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who discovers the application for the first time of a well-known law of nature or property of matter, by means of which a new result in the arts or manufactures is produced, and has pointed out a mode by which it is produced, is entitled to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fortiori, if one discovers the law itself and applies it. The protection extends to the application for the special purpose described; examples include application of steam power, electric current for communication, hot-air blast (Neilson) as discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of known elements producing a new and useful result is patentable as an art
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of instrumentalities before known to produce a new and useful result was held patentable as an art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the implements, elements, and substances were known, arranging them in a novel manner to produce a new useful result can constitute patentable subject matter (example: Roberts v. Dickey — using explosives in wells with novel arrangements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery alone is not patentable; must be connected to a particular medium or contrivance
rubrics_metrics.description: "In its naked, ordinary sense, a discovery is not patentable... It is only where the explorer ... has connected it with some particular medium or mechanical contrivance by which, or through which, it acts on the material world, that he can secure the exclusive control of it under the patent laws."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the discoverer does not 'inhabit' the discovery with a body (means/mode), the discovery remains unpatentable; example: Morton v. New York Eye Infirmary (ether as anæsthetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim that separates the principle from the means and is overly sweeping is void
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that amount to an abstraction (i.e., claiming the use of a motive power for a result without specifying means) are void — the seminal example is the invalidation of Morse's broad eighth claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rejected a claim that would grant exclusive right to all ways of printing at a distance by galvanic current because it would 'stop the progress of invention.' Validity depends on construing the claim with the specification: if the specification supplies the appropriate apparatus/conditions, a narrower construction may save the claim; otherwise it is too broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a patent is limited to what the patentee has established as his invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When the real subject and scope of any patented invention is ascertained, subsequent improvements may be used if they are outside that subject and scope; otherwise they remain within the prior patentee's rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents do not close the progress of invention — they appropriate for a time what the patentee has actually invented and disclosed. Improvements may be independently patentable but still infringing if within prior scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protection is for the disclosed application for a special purpose and duration; the underlying principle remains free for other uses
rubrics_metrics.description: "He is protected only in the enjoyment of the application for the special purpose and object to which it has been newly applied... For every other purpose and end, the principle is free for all mankind to use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor's monopoly is limited in time (statutory term) and to the application/purpose described; other applications of the same principle are not barred by the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty may lie in the application rather than in the means themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of the conception may consist in the discovery and application ... by which a new product in the arts or manufactures is the effect; the means or machinery are material only so far as they effect the identity of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize that the inventive merit often lies in the original conception (application of a principle) rather than mere mechanical contrivances; hence a patent can be supported by the new application even if many parts are old, provided the claimed application produces a previously unknown practical result.
